case_name: Transform Compost Systems Ltd. v. Jayendee Farms Ltd.
text:
IN THE
SUPREME COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA

Citation:

Transform
Compost Systems Ltd. v. Jayendee Farms Ltd.,

2013
BCSC 2579

Date: 20130521

Docket: S135097

Registry: New Westminster

Between:

Transform Compost Systems Ltd. and

Transform Plant Products Inc.

Plaintiffs

And

Jayendee Farms Ltd., John Doppenberg

and Diana Doppenberg

Defendants

And

Transform Compost Systems Ltd.,
Transform Plant Products Inc.,

John Paul, Pieter Vanderpol, Vanderpol’s
Eggs Ltd.

and Vanderpol Enterprises Inc.

Defendants by way of
Counterclaim

Before: The Honourable Mr.
Justice Pearlman

Oral Reasons
for Judgment

Counsel
for the Plaintiffs and Defendants by way of Counterclaim:

D.A.T. Moseley

Counsel
for the Defendants:

G.T. Kosakoski

Place
and Date of Hearing:

Vancouver, B.C.

May 10, 2013

Place
and Date of Judgment:

Vancouver, B.C.

May 21, 2013

[
1
]

THE
COURT:
The
defendants apply for orders that the plaintiffs, Transform Compost Systems Ltd.
and Transform Plant Products Inc. (“Transform”), post security for the
defendants’ costs in the amount of $110,789, and that the defendants have
liberty to apply for dismissal of the plaintiffs’ claims if Transform fails to
post the required security within 21 days of an order of the court requiring
them to do so.

[
2
]

The
plaintiff, Transform Compost Systems Ltd., designs, constructs and operates
waste management and composting facilities.  Transport Plant Products Inc. has
engaged in the business of producing environmentally friendly compost-based
products.  Dr. John Paul, one of the defendants by counterclaim, is the
president of Transform.

[
3
]

The
defendant by counterclaim Vanderpol Enterprises Inc. (“VEI”), is the largest
creditor of Transform.  VEI advanced $556,000 to the plaintiffs for the
composting project, which is the subject of this litigation.  With the
plaintiffs’ acquiescence, VEI oversees the finances of Transform and
effectively controls their financial decisions at present.  The plaintiffs, Dr.
Paul and VEI are all represented by the same counsel in this litigation.

[
4
]

The
defendants John Doppenberg and Diana Doppenberg are the directors of the
defendant Jayendee Farms Ltd., the registered owner of a 19.11 acre farm
located in Abbotsford, British Columbia.

[
5
]

The
parties agree that in 2003 or 2004, Dr. Paul approached Mr. Doppenberg about
using the defendants’ hog farm for an experimental composting project.  However,
in this action the existence, terms and alleged breaches of a somewhat complex
series of oral agreements the plaintiffs say they made with the defendants for
the operation of the composting facility on the defendants’ farm, are all in
issue.

[
6
]

In
their Amended Notice of Civil Claim, the plaintiffs allege that in or around
the summer of 2003, they entered into an oral business agreement with the
defendants to explore new technologies for managing hog and pig manure.  The
plaintiffs say that in furtherance of the business agreement, during the summer
of 2005 they entered into an oral lease agreement with the defendants by which
the parties agreed that Transform would lease the farm property from Jayendee
to establish and operate a composting facility.  According to the plaintiffs,
from the summer of 2005 until 2009 the terms of the lease agreement were:

a)

Jayendee would lease
the property to Transform for an indefinite term;

b)

Transform would
establish and operate the composting business on the property;

c)

Jayendee as the owner
of the property would apply to the requisite municipal and government
authorities for the permit required to operate the composting business on the
property (the “use permit application”);

d)

once the use permit
application was approved, Transform would pay Jayendee base rent of $2,500 per
month and a contribution toward utilities; and

e)

Transform would hire
Mr. and Mrs. Doppenberg as employees to assist on operating the compost
business.

[
7
]

The plaintiffs say that in 2009 the parties
agreed to additional terms for the lease agreement, including:

a)

that Jayendee would
apply for a non-farm use application to permit the property to be used for
purposes other than farming; a soil deposit permit to permit the compositing
business to receive composting ingredients and soil for a flood control berm on
the property; and a rezoning to permit the permanent operation of the
composting business on the property;

b)

that Transform as
Jayendee’s agent would assist Jayendee with these applications; and

c)

as a result of Transform’s
improvements to the property, in the event that the property was sold, the
defendants would provide Transform with reasonable notice to permit the removal
of its machinery, equipment and materials that were not fixtures; and the
defendants would pay Transform an amount equal to 50 percent of the amount by
which the value of the property had increased since the parties made their
business agreement.

[
8
]

The plaintiffs claim that in reliance on the
lease agreement they hired employees, acquired and brought equipment onto the
defendants’ property for the composting business, acquired and stockpiled
composting materials on the property, paid rent, and hired Mr. and Mrs.
Doppenberg as employees of Transform to assist in operating the composting
business.

[
9
]

The plaintiffs plead that in 2010 the requisite
authorities approved a non-farm use application and the soil deposit
application, and that they had laid the groundwork for a successful rezoning
application to permit the permanent operation of a composting facility on the
farm property.

[
10
]

The multiple breaches of contract and torts
alleged by the plaintiffs are set out in paragraphs 15 through 17 of their Amended
Notice of Civil Claim:

15.  Jayendee
and/or the Doppenbergs have conspired and wrongfully interfered with
Transform’s legitimate contractual relations and breached the terms of the
business agreement and the lease agreement with the intent to harm Transform,
particulars of which are,
inter alia
, as follows:

a.

wrongfully using and
converting monies from Transform to pay invoices rendered by Jayendee for
labour never performed by Jayendee, Mr. Doppenberg and Mrs. Doppenberg or any
other employee, agent or servant of Jayendee;

b.

wrongfully resigning
from Transform without warning or reasonable notice;

c.

wrongfully bolting all
or, in the alternative, some of the equipment to concrete slabs on the property
without notice to or approval from Transform and thereafter wrongfully
depriving Transform of their use and further converting the equipment to their
own use;

d.

wrongfully purporting
to increase the rent by approximately 55 percent from $2,500 to $4,500 per
month effective immediately and without prior notice;

e.

wrongfully purporting
to terminate Transform’s lease of the property without reasonable notice;

f.

wrongfully locking the
gates which provide access to the property, thereby physically preventing
Transform from:

i. accessing the property;

ii. operating the composting business on
the property;

iii. removing the equipment from the
property; and

iv. removing the compost material from the
property;

g.   wrongfully refusing to provide
Transform with access to the property for the purposes as aforesaid despite
repeated demands;

h.   wrongfully holding themselves out to
be the full legal and beneficial owners of the property, the equipment, the
greenhouse and all further and other equipment, fixtures and improvements on
the property; and

i.    wrongfully entering into discussions to lease
the property to a direct competitor of Transform while wrongfully holding
themselves out as the full legal and beneficial owners of the property, the
equipment, the greenhouse and all further and other equipment, fixtures and
improvements on the property.

16.  The foregoing acts of the defendants constitute:

a.

breach of the business
agreement and the lease agreement;

b.

an unlawful conspiracy
injurious to Transform;

c.

an unlawful
interference on the contractual relations of Transform;

d.

a wrongful resignation;

e.

wrongful conversion;
and

f.

an unjust enrichment by
the defendants to the deprivation of the plaintiffs.

17.  As a result of the foregoing, Transform has suffered and will
continue suffer irreparable harm, loss and damages, including but not limited
to:

a.

loss of customers;

b.

loss of reputation;

c.

loss of revenue.

[
11
]

The plaintiffs say that as a result of the
defendants’ wrongful denial of access to the farm property and detention of
their equipment, they incurred damages of $205,000 to lease or purchase
replacement equipment in order to relocate and continue their business.  In
addition, they say the defendants wrongfully converted to their own use
composting material worth $150,000.

[
12
]

The plaintiffs attribute their diminished
financial capacity to the defendants’ actions in evicting them from the farm
property and wrongfully detaining or converting equipment and materials
necessary to the operation of their composting enterprise.

[
13
]

For their part, the defendants say that Jayendee
permitted Dr. Paul and/or Transform to construct a prototype compost facility
on the farm, but they never granted Transform or Dr. Paul a right of exclusive
possession of any part of the farm.

[
14
]

The say that between 2005 and 2010 Dr. Paul
expanded Transform’s operations on the farm and sought to obtain approval from
the requisite municipal and governmental authorities for Transform to operate a
permanent compost operation on the farm, and that Transform agreed to pay
Jayendee a monthly licence fee for its non-exclusive use of the farm during
this period.

[
15
]

The defendants allege that in or about June
2010, without their authorization, Dr. Paul applied to the City of Abbotsford
and obtained a soil deposit permit authorizing the deposit on the farm property
of up to 16,000 cubic metres of topsoil and other material from a property
owned by the defendant by counterclaim VEI, the major creditor of Transform.

[
16
]

The defendants allege that the plaintiffs and/or
Dr. Paul, without having obtained the necessary zoning amendment or having met
the conditions for approval by the Agricultural Land Commission, stored large
quantities of clay-like material on the farm property, causing damage to their
home, septic field and agricultural land.

[
17
]

The defendants also contend after the
Agricultural Land Commission declined to approve the operation of a permanent
compositing facility on the farm, the plaintiffs reneged on a previous
agreement to purchase the farm and subsequently failed to make monthly licence
fee payments due to Jayendee for the use of the farm property.

[
18
]

By paras. 1.45 and 1.46 of their Amended Response
to Civil Claim, the defendants plead that in late April 2011 they gave Dr. Paul
notice to quit the farm property and then terminated Dr. Paul’s use of the farm
for cause.

[
19
]

By their Amended Counterclaim, the defendants
plead that Transform and Dr. Paul are indebted to them for $193,500 for
deferred rents and $301,272.50 for deferred wages.  Further, or alternatively,
the defendants also claim for damages for unpaid rents, unpaid wages, waste,
breach of the licence, trespass, breach of contract and defamation.

[
20
]

No trial date has been set.  However, the
parties agree 15 days will be required for the trial of this matter.

[
21
]

Section 236
of the
Business Corporations Act
,
S.B.C. 2002, c. 57, provides statutory authority for the court to order a
corporate plaintiff to provide security for costs:

If a corporation
is the plaintiff in a legal proceeding brought before the court, and if it
appears that the corporation will be unable to pay the costs of the defendant
if the defendant is successful in the defence, the court may require security
to be given by the corporation for those costs, and may stay all legal
proceedings until the security is given.

[
22
]

In
Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform Inc. v.
Canadian Jewish Congress
,
1999 CanLII 5860 (BC SC)
, [1999] 36 CPC (4th) 266 at para.
14
, Mr. Justice
Romilly stated the four-part test that applies where security for costs is
sought against a corporate plaintiff:

1.

Does it appear that the plaintiff company will be unable to pay the
defendants’ costs if the action fails?

2.

If so, has the plaintiff shown that it has exigible assets of
sufficient value to satisfy an award of costs?

3.

Is the court satisfied that the defendants have an arguable defence
to present?

4.

Would an order for costs visit undue hardship on the plaintiff such
that it would prevent the plaintiff’s case from being heard?

[
23
]

As the court explained in
Moulton v. British
Columbia (Ministry of Forests)
,
2009 BCSC 1466
at para.
49
:

[49]   The first three factors are
preconditions to the court’s discretion to order security for costs, and the
fourth factor arises when the court considers exercising its discretion on the
basis of the factors in
Kropp
.  Romilly J. went on to explain what the
court should consider in deciding whether it should exercise its discretion (at
para. 21):

In exercising its discretion to order security for costs, the court
must consider the interests of justice between the parties and balance those
interests to try to insure that the substance of their dispute ends up properly
litigated.  As such, once a
prima facie
case is made out by the
defendants, the court must consider whether an undue hardship would be visited
upon the plaintiff if an award for security for costs was made.  In other
words, would the ordering of security for costs prevent justice from being
done.

[
24
]

In exercising its discretion to make or refuse
an order for security for costs, the court will take into account the
principles and factors stated by the Court of Appeal
in Kropp v. Swaneset
Bay Golf Course Ltd.
(1997),
1997 CanLII 4037 (BC CA)
, 29 B.C.L.R. (3d) 252 at para.
17
:

1.

The court has a complete discretion whether to order security, and
will act in light of all the relevant circumstances;

2.

The possibility or probability that the plaintiff company will be
deterred from pursuing its claim is not without more sufficient reason for not
ordering security;

3.

The court must attempt to balance injustices arising from use of
security as an instrument of oppression to stifle a legitimate claim on the one
hand, and use of impecuniosity as a means of putting unfair pressure on a defendant
on the other;

4.

The court may have regard to the merits of the action, but should
avoid going into detail on the merits unless success or failure appears
obvious;

5.

The court can order any amount of security up to the full amount
claimed, as long as the amount is more than nominal;

6.

Before the court refuses to order security on the ground that it
would unfairly stifle a valid claim, the court must be satisfied that, in all
the circumstances, it is probable that the claim would be stifled; and

7.

The lateness of the application for security is a circumstance which
can properly be taken into account.

[
25
]

The
Kropp
factors are non-exhaustive.
The court has a broad discretion that must be exercised in light of all of the
relevant circumstances.

[
26
]

The defendants submit that they have met the
threshold of establishing a
prima facie
case that the plaintiffs will be
unable to pay an award of costs if their claim is unsuccessful.  The defendants
also argue that Transform has not shown that it has exigible assets sufficient
to pay costs.

[
27
]

The plaintiffs contest each of those assertions
and contend that the defendants have not established an arguable defence to
Transform’s claims in detinue and conversion.

[
28
]

The parties also differ on whether and how the
court should exercise its discretion to make an order based on the principles
discussed in
Kropp
.

[
29
]

Dr. Paul has sworn that an order for security
for costs in the amount sought by the defendants will likely either prevent
Transform from carrying on business or will stifle the plaintiffs’ claims by
preventing them from continuing this litigation.

[
30
]

The defendants submit that the plaintiffs have
not established that an order for security for costs in the amount sought would
stifle their action, because they have adduced no evidence concerning their
capacity to raise or borrow funds to post security either from VEI or any other
source.

[
31
]

I am satisfied that the defendants have
established on a
prima facie
basis that it is unlikely the plaintiffs
will be able to satisfy an award of costs if they are unsuccessful.  First,
dealing with the likely amount of an award of costs, the parties’ estimate of a
15-day trial appears reasonable, as does the defendants’ estimate of their
disbursements in the amount of approximately $18,600.  However, the defendants
have claimed costs at Scale C in their draft bill of costs when calculating
their costs before disbursements in the amount of $82,280.

[
32
]

In my view, although this case has a somewhat
complex factual background, it is unlikely to be a case of more than usual
difficulty.  Accordingly, using the same number of units claimed by the
defendants but using Scale B and accepting the defendants’ anticipated
disbursements, I estimate the likely amount of costs for the purposes of this
application at $75,000 rather than $110,000.

[
33
]

Transform Plant Products Inc. was wound down in
2011 but restored to good standing with the Registrar of Companies in the
summer of 2012 for the purpose of applying for a tax refund.  The amount of
that refund was not disclosed on this application.

[
34
]

Dr. Paul testified on discovery that Transform
Plant Products Inc. had not transacted any business for a year and that he
intended to wind that company down again after it received the tax refund.

[
35
]

The defendants have established on a
prima facie

basis that Transform Plant Products Inc. may not be able to pay an award of
costs.

[
36
]

Transform is indebted to VEI for $556,000.
Although VEI has agreed not to collect on its loans at this time and has
discharged its security, it oversees the plaintiffs’ finances and has not
relinquished its right to seek repayment at some time in the future.  Transform
is also indebted to one of its suppliers for work done on the farm property in
the amount of $60,000.

[
37
]

Transform has been attempting to rebuild its
business since its eviction from the defendants’ farm.  Between January 1, 2013,
and April 30, 2013, it earned revenue of $45,136.52 from the sale of compost.
In addition, Transform secured a design contract for $60,000 and expects, but
has not yet received, two purchase orders for equipment valued at approximately
$347,000.

[
38
]

However, in assessing the plaintiffs’ ability to
pay an award of costs, I am unable to attach much weight to anticipated
purchase orders that have not yet materialized.

[
39
]

Further, there are no financial statements or
other evidence before the court of the expenses Transform has incurred in order
to generate revenue from compost sales or will incur in performing other work.

[
40
]

Taking into account Transform’s diminished
financial circumstances, the potential that one of the plaintiffs, Transform
Plant Products Inc. may cease to operate at all before these proceedings
conclude, and the amount of any likely award of costs, I find that the
defendants have shown on a
prima facie
basis that the plaintiffs would
be unable to pay an award of costs.  In making that finding, I have taken into
account that there are no other actions and no outstanding judgments against
the plaintiffs.

[
41
]

Before turning to the question of whether the
plaintiffs have shown that they have exigible assets sufficient to satisfy any
potential award of costs, I will consider whether the defendants have an
arguable defence to the plaintiffs’ claims.

[
42
]

While the threshold on an application for
security for costs for an arguable defence is quite low, more is required than
a general denial:
Integrated Contractors Ltd. v. Leduc Development Ltd.
,

2009 BCSC 965
at para.
27
.

[
43
]

Here, the defendants have pleaded that as result
of the plaintiffs’ failure to pay the rent and repair damage they had caused to
the farm property, Jayendee terminated the plaintiffs’ licence for cause.  The
defendants have also pleaded that they gave the plaintiffs reasonable notice to
vacate and reasonable access for the removal of their equipment and material
from the farm property.

[
44
]

In response to the plaintiffs’ allegation that
they wrongfully bolted Transform’s equipment to the farm property and thereby
converted that equipment to their own use, the defendants have pleaded that any
machinery that was bolted to the property was bolted by Dr. Paul as part of the
normal operation of such machinery.

[
45
]

Whether the defendants had cause to terminate
the lease or licence, whether they gave reasonable notice to vacate in the
particular circumstances of this case, and whether the defendants wrongfully
detained or converted property of the plaintiffs, are all matters to be
determined by the trial judge.

[
46
]

At this stage, I am satisfied that the
defendants have an arguable defence to the plaintiffs’ claims, including their
claims for conversion and detinue.

[
47
]

Have the plaintiffs shown that they have
exigible assets of real and substantial character sufficient to satisfy a costs
award?  Transform has 16 pieces of equipment (the “valued equipment”), which
have been appraised by an experienced heavy equipment appraiser at a current
fair market value of $395,477.

[
48
]

The plaintiffs owe Vancouver City Savings Credit
Union $42,370 on a line of credit secured by a general security agreement
charging all of the plaintiffs’ present and after-acquired personal property.
In addition, five pieces of the valued equipment are charged by specific
security agreements.

[
49
]

After deduction of all of the amounts owed by
Transform on the line of credit and the five pieces of equipment subject to
purchase or lease agreements, the total value remaining in the valued equipment
is $197,830.  That amount substantially exceeds the defendants’ potential
costs, which I have estimated in the amount of $75,000.

[
50
]

Transform is making all of the monthly payments
on the line of credit and the equipment purchase agreements.  Until recently,
VEI also held a PPSA security agreement charging all of the plaintiffs’ present
and after-acquired personal property as security for its loans to Transform
totalling $556,000.

[
51
]

VEI discharged its security agreement on May 9,
2013.  VEI has also agreed with the plaintiffs not to collect on its loan at
this time, and is prepared to enter into a consent order by which it would
subordinate its claims to the loans to any judgment that the defendants may
obtain against the plaintiffs on their counterclaim.

[
52
]

VEI has attached as an exhibit to the affidavit
of George Leroux, one of its directors and officers, an extract from the notes
to its financial statements for the year ended August 31, 2012.  That note
indicates that VEI had then determined that its loans receivable from Transform
were no longer collectable, because the plaintiffs’ underlying assets were
insufficient to repay the amount due to VEI and that the company had included
in its loan impairment provisions for 2012 the full $556,000 due from
Transform.

[
53
]

I accept Mr. Leroux’s explanation that delay in
filing the discharge of VEI’s PPSA security agreement was due to
inadvertence.

[
54
]

In the result, Transform has established that it
has exigible assets of almost $198,000, an amount substantially in excess of
what would be required to satisfy any potential order for costs.  Accordingly,
the plaintiffs have shown that one of the three pre-conditions to the court’s
exercise of its discretion to order security for costs is not met.

[
55
]

The defendants’ application for an order
requiring the plaintiffs to post security for costs is therefore dismissed.

[
56
]

The defendants made a submission that Dr. Paul
failed to disclose the existence of the security agreements charging the valued
equipment and other personal property of the plaintiffs and gave false
affidavit evidence that there were no security agreements over the valued
equipment.

[
57
]

The defendants argued that Dr. Paul and the
plaintiffs intended to mislead the Court, or gave false evidence with a
reckless disregard for its truth, and that this constituted reprehensible
conduct warranting the court’s rebuke by an order for the special costs of this
application in any event of the cause.

[
58
]

Where the court finds that a party has
deliberately attempted to mislead by giving false evidence, that conduct may
found an award of special costs:
Laface v. McWilliams
,
2005 BCSC 1766

at para.
43
, and
Webber v. Canadian Aviation Insurance Managers Ltd.
,

2003 BCSC 274 (CanLII)
, [2003] B.C.J. No. 381.

[
59
]

In his Affidavit No. 5 sworn May 7, 2013, Dr.
Paul identified four of the five pieces of the valued equipment on which
Transform makes monthly lease or purchase agreement payments and the amounts
owing on each of those agreements.  He also deposed there were no amounts owing
to other parties regarding the purchase of the valued equipment and that there
were no security agreements over the valued equipment.

[
60
]

A search by the defendants of the Personal
Property Registry revealed that on May 7, 2013, there were a total of nine
security agreements registered against Transform Compost Systems Ltd. and the
assets described in those security agreements.

[
61
]

In addition to the Vancouver City Savings Credit
Union’s security agreement and the VEI security agreement that was discharged
on May 9, 2013, the remaining security agreements either charged single pieces
of equipment included in the valued property or related to other equipment
owned by Transform.

[
62
]

On May 9, 2013, Dr. Paul swore his sixth
affidavit, in which he deposed that he did not recall signing a document
charging all of Transform’s present or after-acquired personal property; that
he did not understand all personal property to include equipment; and that he
did not understand that VEI had a security agreement, because Mr. Leroux had
informed him, and he believed, that VEI had written off its loans in 2012.

[
63
]

Dr. Paul also corrected his previous admission
of the amount owing on one of the pieces of the valued equipment and attached a
copy of the relevant lease agreement.  He identified additional pieces of
equipment held by Transform that are not included in the valued equipment and
provided copies of many of the financing contracts relating to Transform’s
equipment.

[
64
]

Dr. Paul’s explanations for the errors in his
fifth affidavit reveal an initial lack of attention to ensuring the accuracy of
his evidence relating to the plaintiffs’ financial affairs.   That is a cause for
a concern, bearing in mind that he is the president of Transform and is
directly involved in the plaintiffs’ operations and this litigation.

[
65
]

Dr. Paul must have understood the importance on
this application of accurately identifying Transform’s exigible assets.
However, on a balance of probabilities, I am not persuaded that Dr. Paul’s
errors and omissions are attributable to a deliberate attempt to mislead the Court,
or a reckless disregard for the truth rather than a flawed memory and a lack of
sophistication in commercial matters.

[
66
]

Once his errors were brought to his attention,
Dr. Paul promptly swore an affidavit correcting his previous evidence and
providing full disclosure of the amounts owing on the valued equipment and the
security agreements charging that equipment.  Nonetheless, as a result of the
misinformation contained in Dr. Paul’s fifth affidavit, both parties were put
to additional and unnecessary time and expense to correct his errors.

[
67
]

In these circumstances, I find this to be an
appropriate case to depart from the usual rule that costs follow the event and
to order that the plaintiffs and the defendants will each bear their own costs
of this application.

[
68
]

That concludes my Reasons for Judgment on this
application.  The defendants’ application is dismissed.  Thank you.

[
69
]

MR. KOSAKOSKI:  Thank you.

[
70
]

MR. MOSELEY:  Thank you, My Lord.

“PEARLMAN J.”
